newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian banks seen adding to share market boom.
newsitem.headline: Russian banks seen adding to share market boom.

text.p: Russians have begun investing in a share market dominated by Westerners but long-term investors sitting on new purchases and strong demand during a market boom are limiting liquidity, analysts said on Monday.

Russian investors, led by banks which have made tidy profits on the lucrative Treasury bill market, have begun investing in Russian shares, a much smaller market which may offer some of the yields that T-bills no longer can.
"Isn't it wonderful?" said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow. "It's another reason 1997 is sizing up to be a spectacular year for the shares market."
Yields in the 235 trillion rouble ($42 billion) government securities market, with $1 billion daily turnover, have fallen below 30 percent from close to 200 percent early last year.

The vastly smaller Russian Trading System (RTS) equities market sees $30-$50 million in daily turnover. The RTS index of 24 leading shares set a new record on Monday, rising to 304.90, compared with below 200 at the end of last year.
One senior trader said total daily turnover of Russian shares, including unreported domestic trades and trades of American Depositary Receipts abroad, could top $500 million.
Many analysts put the figure closer to $100 million.
Traders said that the new flow of funds was significant enough to move the market -- $10 million in bank funds last week by one estimate -- but pales in comparison to what it could be.

"Banks are looking for some other niche for high returns," said one trader. Operators said the banks, chiefly interested in the most liquid shares, were steadily increasing their investment after years of waiting by equities dealers.

Christopher Granville, director of research at United City Bank, said Russian banks represented up to 30 percent of the free float in some leading stocks and could be expected to be active traders in equities.

But the major foreign funds which have driven the market up about 50 percent since the beginning of the year are longer-term investors and market liquidity is still tight despite increasingly higher trading volumes, Granville said.
"Most fund managers don't see this as a tradeable market. In Russia we think that spreads of less than five percent are fantastically grown up. They are looking for growth over time."
Newly created Russian and foreign-owned funds are also targeting Russian retail investors with cash to spare.

In recent years domestic investors have had a choice between low-yielding savings bank accounts in depreciating roubles or holding dollars in cash, unless they were super-rich and could move their money off-shore.
Companies such as Pioneer and Credit Suisse have launched accessible mutual funds in the last few months. Most of these invest in T-bills but at least one is investing in equities.

Equity analysts say as much as $1 billion has poured into Russian equities since the beginning of the year as daily volume has almost doubled and market capitalisation jumped to more than $54 billion from $37 billion at the beginning of the year.
But the sharp growth in stock prices has made investors and traders careful about buying and selling -- especially selling.

"Anytime someone buys (a large lot), that has driven the price up," said Nail, predicting continued market growth. "But we have seen some major sellers that have not pushed prices down. The market has absorbed all the paper it can."
